rubric.why: Awards the definition’s central idea: science is organized knowledge about the natural world.
rubric.description: Science is collective knowledge about natural phenomena and events.
rubric.how: Look for collective knowledge and its connection to nature or natural phenomena.

rubric.why: The answer must name both main groups and distinguish living from non-living things.
rubric.description: Biological sciences study living things; physical sciences study non-living things.
rubric.how: Require both groups and the living/non-living distinction.

modelAnswer: Science is a collective knowledge about the natural phenomena, processes and events occurring around us. The biological sciences which deal with the living things. The physical sciences which are about the study of non-living things.

rubric.why: Recognizes Physics as a fundamental science and identifies what it studies.
rubric.description: Physics studies the constituents of the universe, including matter, energy, space and time.
rubric.how: Look for Physics as fundamental science and key constituents of the universe.

rubric.why: Requires examples of branches of Physics, not just a description of the subject.
rubric.description: Names at least two branches of Physics.
rubric.how: Accept any two distinct branches named in the textbook answer.

modelAnswer: Physics is the fundamental science that deals with the constituents of the universe, that is, matter, energy, space, time and their mutual relationships and interactions. Some branches of Physics are Mechanics, Heat and thermodynamics, Acoustics, Optics, Electromagnetism, Quantum Mechanics, Relativistic Mechanics, Nuclear Physics, Particle Physics, Astronomy, Cosmology and Solid State Physics.

rubric.why: Awards the initial stages of the method: recognizing a problem, observing it and proposing a hypothesis.
rubric.description: Identify the problem, gather observations and propose a hypothesis.
rubric.how: Look for the problem, observation/information gathering and hypothesis stages.

rubric.why: Awards the testing and later stages: experiment, data analysis, conclusion as theory and repeated testing toward a law.
rubric.description: Test the hypothesis, analyze data and reach a theory; repeated tests can lead to a law.
rubric.how: Require the experiment, data, theory and law stages to be represented.

modelAnswer: 1. Identify or recognize an issue or a problem. 2. Gather information through observations of its various aspects. 3. Propose an explanation or a guess work known as hypothesis. 4. Perform experiment or collect evidences to test the hypothesis. 5. Record, organize and analyze gathered data, plotting and interpreting graphs to reach at a conclusion which is called a theory. 6. Repeated tests of the theory to wide range of similar issues then lead towards the formulation of a law.

rubric.why: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation or guess, not an established law.
rubric.description: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation or guess.
rubric.how: Look for both the tentative nature and the idea of an explanation or guess.

rubric.why: Awards the textbook example and its proposed reason.
rubric.description: Shadows of opaque objects form in the path of light because light travels in a straight line.
rubric.how: Require shadows/opaque objects and the straight-line travel of light.

modelAnswer: Propose an explanation or a guess work known as hypothesis. From the above example, we assume that shadows of opaque objects are formed when they come in the path of light because light travels in a straight line.

rubric.why: Identifies a theory as a logical explanation of causes and effects.
rubric.description: A theory logically explains the causes and effects of an event or issue in nature.
rubric.how: Look for a logical explanation connecting causes and effects.

rubric.why: Distinguishes a law as a repeatedly tested, generally accepted statement about nature that explains observations and can predict behaviour.
rubric.description: A law is a repeatedly tested, generally accepted statement that explains observations and can make predictions.
rubric.how: Require repeated testing or general acceptance, plus its explanatory or predictive role.

modelAnswer: It is a logical explanation of the causes and effects of an issue or an event that occurs in nature. When a theory has been tested many times and generally accepted as true, it is called a law. The law is such a statement regarding the behaviour of nature which explains the observations and experiments of the past and can predict about other aspects of nature.

rubric.why: States that theories or laws are human-made ideas about how things work, rather than ultimate truths.
rubric.description: Theories and laws are man-made ideas about how things work.
rubric.how: Look for the man-made nature of theories or laws and their account of how things work.

rubric.why: Explains that future scientific advances and new evidence may overturn or modify them.
rubric.description: They may be disproved or modified as science advances and new facts emerge.
rubric.how: Require the possibility of change and its connection to future scientific advances or new facts.

modelAnswer: The theories or laws of Physics are man-made ideas about the way the things work. They are liable to be disproved or modified with the future advances in science which brings fresh facts and new insights about the natural and physical world.

rubric.why: States that theories or laws are human-made ideas about how things work.
rubric.description: Theories and laws are man-made ideas about how things work.
rubric.how: Look for the man-made nature of theories or laws and their account of how things work.

rubric.why: Explains that future scientific advances and new evidence may overturn or modify existing laws.
rubric.description: Existing laws may be disproved or modified as science advances and new facts emerge.
rubric.how: Require the possibility of change and its connection to future scientific advances or new facts.

modelAnswer: The theories or laws of Physics are man-made ideas about the way the things work. They are liable to be disproved or modified with the future advances in science which brings fresh facts and new insights about the natural and physical world.

rubric.why: Awards one valid job example with a relevant use of scientific knowledge.
rubric.description: Gives one suitable example, such as a civil engineer designing a bridge or a software engineer designing a smartphone application.
rubric.how: Accept a job paired with its relevant task from the textbook examples.

rubric.why: Awards a second valid job example demonstrating another use of scientific knowledge.
rubric.description: Gives a second suitable example, such as an aviation engineer selecting materials for an aeroplane.
rubric.how: Accept another valid job-and-task example; do not award twice for repeating the same example.

modelAnswer: A civil engineer designs a bridge that can withstand strong winds, earthquakes, intense weather conditions and heavy traffic. A software engineer designs a user friendly application of a smartphone. An aviation engineer looks for lighter material which can withstand sudden and severe disturbances and extreme weather conditions during the flight of an aeroplane.
